To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a strong cell-mediated immune response against a SIV split vaccine or SIV itself is inducable in macaques without any humoral immune response, and that a low dose SIV challenge does not protect against a subsequent high dose SIV challenge.

low dose SIV inoculations induce a SIV-specific T-helper cell response in the absence of a humoral immune response, and that this cellular immune response cannot protect the animals against infection and disease development.
low doses of infectious or inactivated SIV induced a strong CMI, which was neither TH1- nor TH2-like.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the induction of an effective CMI against HIV/SIV.
the development of a safe and effective SIV vaccine, which should induce a strong cell-mediated immune response.
the induction of a strong CMI by different immunization protocols and its correlation to the outcome of an intravenous SIV-challenge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the low-dose SIV immunization strategy failed to induce protection against SIV challenge.
the induction of a strong CMI is not sufficient to prevent infection with SIV.
the CMI response induced in macaques is not sufficient to protect against HIV/SIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
low doses of a split-SIV vaccine or of infectious SIV induce a strong CML in macaques without the development of neutralizing antibodies.
low dose SIV immunization is not sufficient to induce protection in macaques.
the induction of an SIV-specific TH proliferation by immunization with a low dose of the split-vaccine or by low dose infection with SIV is possible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
low doses of SIV can induce strong cellular immunity in macaques, which is not able to prevent subsequent SIV infection.
the induction of a CMI in macaque monkeys by immunization with low doses of SIV does not confer protection against infection and disease development.
a CMI response is not sufficient to protect against SIV infection in macaques.
